notes:
Task and constraints: Convert an uppercase Excel column title into its positive 1-indexed number.
Idea: Start value at zero and for each ch multiply the accumulated value by 26, then add ch's A-based digit plus one.
Technique and why it applies: Horner evaluation of base 26 decodes the title left to right without storing intermediate digits.
Invariant: After each character, value equals the numeric column index represented by the processed prefix.
Edge cases: A becomes 1; AB becomes 28; ZY becomes 701. The method assumes uppercase letters as specified; an empty title returns zero.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop reads each character once and updates one integer accumulator.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decode an uppercase Excel title into its 1-indexed column number.
Idea: Iterate i over columnTitle, multiplying value by 26 and adding charAt(i)-'A'+1 for each letter.
Technique and why it applies: Left-to-right base-26 accumulation folds each new digit into the prefix value.
Invariant: value is the column number of the prefix through index i after each iteration.
Edge cases: A returns 1, AB returns 28, and ZY returns 701. Java int arithmetic can overflow for titles longer than the problem's numeric constraints allow; an empty title returns zero.
Complexity: Time O(n), auxiliary space O(1).
complexity_reason: The for loop reads n chars and retains only the running int value and index.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count decimal trailing zeroes in n!, without constructing the enormous factorial.
Idea: Repeatedly divide n by five and add each quotient to count until n becomes zero.
Technique and why it applies: Every factor of five pairs with a factor of two to form a zero; higher powers contribute additional fives counted by successive quotients.
Invariant: count equals floor(original n/5)+floor(original n/25)+... for the processed divisors.
Edge cases: n=5 returns 1; n=25 returns 6; n=0 skips the loop and returns 0.
Complexity: Time O(log_5 n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each pass divides n by five, so the number of iterations is logarithmic.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the number of trailing zeroes in n! using integer operations rather than computing n!.
Idea: While n>0, divide n by 5 and add the quotient to count; return the accumulated total.
Technique and why it applies: Successive divisions count multiples of 5, 25, 125, and so on, including numbers contributing multiple factors of five.
Invariant: After each division, count contains the sum of all quotients already removed from the original n.
Edge cases: n=5 gives 1; n=25 gives 6; n=0 returns 0 immediately. Java integer division truncates toward zero, which matches the nonnegative input.
Complexity: Time O(log_5 n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop repeatedly divides one integer by five and stores only count and n.

notes:
Task and constraints: Implement BSTIterator that emits BST values in ascending order with O(h) auxiliary storage.
Idea: _push_left pushes a node and its left descendants; next pops the smallest pending node, pushes the left spine of its right child, and returns its value. hasNext tests stack truthiness.
Technique and why it applies: An explicit stack simulates recursive inorder traversal while retaining only the active path and deferred ancestors.
Invariant: The stack's top is the next unvisited inorder node.
Edge cases: A null root initializes an empty stack; a leaf is popped once; calling next after exhaustion raises an empty-list pop error, so callers should check hasNext.
Complexity: Initialization O(h), next O(1) amortized, space O(h).
complexity_reason: Each tree node is pushed and popped once; the stack stores at most a root-to-leaf path.

notes:
Task and constraints: Design an ascending BST iterator with amortized O(1) next and O(h) auxiliary space.
Idea: Constructor calls pushLeft(root); next pops the stack top, pushes the left spine of that node's right subtree, and returns node.val. hasNext checks whether the deque is nonempty.
Technique and why it applies: The explicit stack preserves inorder traversal state without storing all sorted values.
Invariant: stack.peek() is the smallest node not yet returned.
Edge cases: Null root gives no next item; a leaf is returned once; next on an empty ArrayDeque throws NoSuchElementException from pop.
Complexity: Initialization O(h), next O(1) amortized, space O(h).
complexity_reason: Every node enters and leaves the deque once, with at most h nodes stored simultaneously.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum starting health to cross a nonempty dungeon grid moving only right/down while health stays at least one.
Idea: dp[c] represents required health for the cell below; traverse rows and columns backward, setting dp[c] to max(1,min(down,right)-dungeon[r][c]), with dp[cols-1]=1 at the destination boundary.
Technique and why it applies: Reverse dynamic programming computes the minimum health needed before entering each cell, compressing a grid table to one row.
Invariant: Before updating column c, dp[c] is the requirement from below and dp[c+1] is the requirement from the right.
Edge cases: The example returns 7; a positive room can reduce required health but never below 1; empty grids are not guarded and are outside expected input.
Complexity: Time O(mn), space O(n).
complexity_reason: The nested loops visit every grid cell once and dp holds cols+1 values.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute minimum initial health for a nonempty dungeon, with right/down moves and strictly positive health along the path.
Idea: Fill long[] dp with a large sentinel, seed dp[cols-1]=1, then scan from bottom-right and update each cell from the minimum of down/right requirements minus its dungeon value, clamped to one.
Technique and why it applies: Backward DP expresses each cell's requirement from its best successor and needs only one row of state.
Invariant: During the reverse scan, dp[c] still represents the cell below and dp[c+1] already represents the current row's right neighbor.
Edge cases: The sample yields 7; positive cells cannot reduce need below 1; long arithmetic and a large sentinel reduce intermediate overflow risk before casting the answer to int.
Complexity: Time O(mn), space O(n).
complexity_reason: The nested loops process rows*cols cells and the long array contains cols+1 entries.

notes:
Task and constraints: Arrange nonnegative integers so concatenation is lexicographically maximal; sorting must compare concatenated pairs rather than numeric values.
Idea: Convert nums to strings, sort with cmp_to_key comparing b+a against a+b, join parts, and normalize a leading-zero result to "0".
Technique and why it applies: The pairwise concatenation comparator puts a before b exactly when a+b is at least as large as b+a.
Invariant: After sorting, adjacent parts are ordered by the comparator, so their concatenation is maximal under this rule.
Edge cases: [3,30,34,5,9] yields "9534330"; all zeros normalize to "0"; empty nums produces an empty result because result is false.
Complexity: Time O(n log n * L), space O(nL).
complexity_reason: Sorting makes O(n log n) comparisons over strings of length at most L, then join builds the result.

notes:
Task and constraints: Arrange nonnegative integers to form the largest concatenated number.
Idea: Convert each number to a string, sort parts using comparison of b+a against a+b, return "0" for an empty array or a first part equal to zero, otherwise append parts to StringBuilder.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing both possible concatenation orders determines which string should precede the other for the largest result.
Invariant: The sorted array is ordered so swapping any adjacent pair would not improve their concatenation.
Edge cases: The sample produces "9534330"; [0,0] returns "0"; an empty array also returns "0". String concatenation inside the comparator creates temporary strings.
Complexity: Time O(n log n * L), space O(nL).
complexity_reason: The sort performs O(n log n) concatenation comparisons, and the output builder stores all digits.

notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse word order in a character list in place, using constant extra space and single spaces between words.
Idea: reverse(left,right) swaps the full array first; then scan through each separator and the end sentinel, reversing each word segment and advancing start.
Technique and why it applies: Reversing the whole sequence and then each word restores letters within words while keeping the word blocks reversed.
Invariant: After each segment boundary, all words before start have their letters restored and remain in reversed word order.
Edge cases: A single word returns unchanged; "the sky" becomes "sky the"; empty input safely calls reverse(0,-1) and executes no swaps.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The whole-array reversal and per-word reversals together touch each character only a constant number of times.

notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse the order of words in a char array in place without allocating another character array.
Idea: reverse the entire array, scan through spaces and the terminal index, reverse each word interval, and set start to the next character.
Technique and why it applies: The first reversal changes word order and reversals of individual words restore each word's internal character order.
Invariant: At each separator, the completed prefix contains correctly spelled words in reversed order.
Edge cases: A single word is unchanged; "the sky" becomes "sky the"; the condition i==s.length prevents reading s[s.length]. Java char[] is modified directly and uses constant auxiliary storage.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The helper swaps characters in place, and the scan checks each position once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return each distinct length-10 DNA substring occurring at least twice.
Idea: For every valid start i, slice s[i:i+10]; place unseen substrings in seen and repeated ones in repeated, then return repeated as a list.
Technique and why it applies: Two sets separate first occurrence from duplicates and ensure a substring appears only once in the result.
Invariant: seen contains every window encountered, while repeated contains exactly those seen at least twice so far.
Edge cases: Strings shorter than ten produce []; the second occurrence adds a sequence to repeated; later occurrences do not duplicate it. Python set iteration makes output order unspecified.
Complexity: Expected O(n) for fixed length ten, space O(n).
complexity_reason: The loop creates at most n-9 fixed-length windows and both sets store distinct windows.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find unique DNA strings of length ten that occur more than once in s.
Idea: Slide i while i+10<=s.length(), create substring(i,i+10), add it to seen, and when add returns false place it in insertion-ordered repeated; return repeated as a list.
Technique and why it applies: Hash sets detect repeats in expected constant time, and LinkedHashSet suppresses duplicate results while preserving discovery order.
Invariant: seen records every window already visited, and repeated records each sequence that has been encountered again.
Edge cases: Length below ten returns an empty list; a third occurrence does not duplicate output; substring's end index is safe due to the loop condition. Java creates a string for each window.
Complexity: Expected O(n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: The loop constructs each valid ten-character substring and stores unique windows in two sets.

notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize profit from at most k buy/sell transactions; when k is at least half the number of days, every profitable rise can be taken.
Idea: Return zero for short input or k=0; use positive adjacent differences for large k; otherwise update buy[t] and sell[t] for each price and transaction count.
Technique and why it applies: State DP tracks best profit after a buy or sell, while the unlimited-transactions shortcut removes the k dimension when it cannot bind.
Invariant: buy[t] is best balance after a t-th buy and sell[t] is best completed profit using at most t sales after processed prices.
Edge cases: k=0 returns 0; [2,4,1], k=2 returns 2 through shortcut; falling prices yield zero profit. buy updates precede sell updates for the same day as written.
Complexity: O(nk), or O(n) in shortcut; space O(k).
complexity_reason: The DP loops over n prices and k states, using two arrays of k+1 values.

notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize stock profit with at most k transactions; large k permits collecting every positive day-to-day rise.
Idea: Handle n<2 or k=0, use adjacent gains if k>=n/2, else initialize buy to a negative sentinel and update buy[t] and sell[t] per price.
Technique and why it applies: The two DP arrays capture holding after a buy and profit after a sale for each transaction limit.
Invariant: sell[t] retains the best completed profit using at most t transactions through the processed prices; buy[t] retains the best buy-state.
Edge cases: [2,4,1] with k=2 returns 2 via the shortcut; k=0 returns 0; Integer.MIN_VALUE/2 is a safe negative starting sentinel for ordinary bounded prices. Java int profit assumes problem constraints avoid overflow.
Complexity: O(nk), or O(n) when k is large; space O(k).
complexity_reason: The inner DP performs k updates for each of n prices, with two arrays of length k+1.

notes:
Task and constraints: Rotate nums right by k steps in place, with O(1) extra storage.
Idea: Return on empty input, reduce k modulo length, reverse the entire list, reverse the first k items, then reverse the remaining suffix.
Technique and why it applies: Three reversals move the final k elements to the front while restoring order within both resulting blocks.
Invariant: After the first reversal the original order is reversed; after the second and third, the two blocks are internally restored and swapped.
Edge cases: [1,2,3,4,5,6,7], k=3 becomes [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]; k=0 reverses whole then reverses all back; empty input avoids modulo by zero.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each of the three reverse calls swaps at most half of its interval and uses constant local state.

notes:
Task and constraints: Rotate an int array right by k positions in place with constant extra space.
Idea: Return for an empty array, normalize k with modulo length, reverse the full array, then reverse [0,k-1] and [k,n-1] using the helper.
Technique and why it applies: The whole-array reversal exchanges block order; reversing each block restores the order of its elements.
Invariant: After all three calls, the original suffix of length k precedes the original prefix of length n-k.
Edge cases: The example with k=3 yields [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]; k equal to array length becomes zero; empty arrays return before modulo.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The three in-place reversals together perform O(n) swaps and allocate no auxiliary array.

notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse all 32 bits of an integer, including leading zero bits in its 32-bit representation.
Idea: Repeat 32 times, shift result left, append n's least-significant bit with OR, then shift n right.
Technique and why it applies: Fixed-width bit extraction constructs the reversed representation one bit at a time.
Invariant: After i iterations, result contains the first i original low-order bits in reversed order in its low i positions.
Edge cases: n=0 returns 0; the example maps 43261596 to 964176192; Python right shift of negative integers is sign-extending, so the implementation relies on the judge supplying a 32-bit nonnegative value.
Complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop always runs exactly 32 times and uses only n, result, and a loop counter.

notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse the 32-bit pattern of an integer and return the reversed bits in an int.
Idea: Run 32 iterations, shift result left and OR in n&1, then use unsigned right shift n >>>= 1 to expose the next bit.
Technique and why it applies: A fixed 32-step shift-and-append process reverses bit order without converting to a string.
Invariant: After i rounds, result's lowest i bits are the first i bits extracted from n in reverse significance order.
Edge cases: Zero remains zero; the example yields 964176192; unsigned shift ensures sign bits do not keep propagating when n is negative. Java int represents the returned 32-bit pattern even if its signed value is negative.
Complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop performs 32 fixed bit updates and stores only two integer values.
